PERSONAL LIABILITY OF SUPERVISORS, OFFICERS AND PUBLIC OFFICIALS FOR A TERMINATION (GOV. CODE §§ 12926(D), 12940(A), (H), (I), 820.2; LAB. CODE §§ 558.1, 1102.5; RENO V. BAIRD; JONES V. LODGE AT TORREY PINES; MIKLOSY V. REGENTS; CALDWELL V. MONTOYA; REYNOLDS V. BEMENT; MARTINEZ V. COMBS; VORIS V. LAMPERT) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. provides this information sheet to Jordan Lee to describe what California statutes and the published decisions of the California Supreme Court say about a single question that arises when an employment relationship ends: who, besides the employing entity itself, the law makes answerable in damages for the termination and for wages left unpaid at the end of the employment.

It covers the definition of “employer” in the Fair Employment and Housing Act and the Act’s “agent” language; the holding of Reno v. Baird that nonemployer individuals may not be sued under the FEHA for discrimination, and the reasoning about “personnel management” decisions on which that holding rests; the same Court’s treatment of the FEHA’s aiding-and-abetting provision; the extension of the rule to the common law tort of wrongful discharge in violation of public policy, in Reno itself and in Miklosy v. Regents; the parallel holding for retaliation in Jones v. Lodge at Torrey Pines Partnership; the questions those opinions expressly left open; the separate discretionary-act immunity that Government Code section 820.2 gives a public employee, applied to a board’s vote to terminate a chief executive in Caldwell v. Montoya; the common law rule on personal liability of corporate agents for unpaid wages in Reynolds v. Bement as that rule was confirmed and confined in Martinez v. Combs; the refusal in Voris v. Lampert to recognize a conversion claim for unpaid wages against an individual officer; the statutory liability that Labor Code section 558.1 places on an owner, director, officer or managing agent for violations of a list of Labor Code sections that includes the waiting-time penalty statute; and the phrase “any person acting on behalf of the employer” in the whistleblower statute, Labor Code section 1102.5.

This sheet states what the authorities say. It does not evaluate any separation, does not identify who may or may not be named in any proceeding, does not state whether any claim exists, and does not tell any reader what to do.

HOW THE FEHA NAMES THE PARTY WHOSE CONDUCT IT FORBIDS, AND THE “AGENT” LANGUAGE IN THE DEFINITION OF “EMPLOYER”
The Fair Employment and Housing Act’s core discrimination prohibition is written against a single actor. Government Code section 12940 opens by declaring what “it is an unlawful employment practice” to do, and subdivision (a) then directs the prohibition at “an employer”: it is that party which may not, because of the listed characteristics, refuse to hire, bar, or discharge a person from employment.

The word “employer” is itself defined. Government Code section 12926, subdivision (d), provides that the term includes any person regularly employing five or more persons — and also “any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly.” For many years that agent clause supplied the textual argument that a supervisor who carried out a discharge was himself or herself an “employer” within the Act, and therefore personally suable. The clauses that follow describe how the California Supreme Court resolved that argument.

RENO V. BAIRD: NONEMPLOYER INDIVIDUALS MAY NOT BE SUED UNDER THE FEHA FOR A DISCRIMINATORY DISCHARGE
In Reno v. Baird (1998) 18 Cal.4th 640, a registered nurse alleged she had been discharged because of her medical condition and sued both the business entities that employed her and individual defendants, including her supervisor, alleging that the individuals had acted as agents of the businesses and were therefore also “employers” under the FEHA. The supervisor obtained summary judgment; the Court of Appeal reversed, holding that supervisory agents could be sued; and the California Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeal.

The Court stated its conclusion at the outset and again at the end of its FEHA analysis: the statute permits suit against employers but not against individuals, and individuals who do not themselves qualify as employers may not be sued under the FEHA for alleged discriminatory acts. In reaching that result the Court approved the contrary-to-the-Court-of-Appeal holding of Janken v. GM Hughes Electronics (1996) 46 Cal.App.4th 55.

THE REASONING: DISCRIMINATION ARISES FROM PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT DECISIONS, AND THE LEGISLATURE BALANCED ENFORCEMENT AGAINST THE BURDEN OF LITIGATION ON INDIVIDUALS
Reno rested on a distinction the FEHA itself draws between harassment and discrimination. Quoting Janken, the Court explained that harassment consists of conduct outside the scope of necessary job performance, while making decisions is conduct essential to personnel management — a supervisor can refrain from harassing, but cannot refrain from making the personnel decisions that may later be claimed to be discriminatory. The same passage lists the kinds of actions the Legislature treated as commonly necessary personnel management: hiring and firing, job or project assignments, promotion or demotion, performance evaluations, and deciding who will be laid off.

The Court also gave a structural reason. The FEHA exempts small employers from the discrimination provisions, and the Court found it incongruous to exempt a small employer while exposing an individual supervisor. It described the resulting rule as a legislative balance between eliminating workplace discrimination and limiting the burden of litigation on individuals, noting that supervisors who cause their employers to incur liability may still face demotion or discharge even though they do not bear the cost of defending the suit.

THE FEHA’S AIDING-AND-ABETTING PROVISION AND WHY IT WAS HELD NOT TO REACH A SUPERVISOR’S OWN PERSONNEL DECISIONS
Government Code section 12940, subdivision (i), makes it an unlawful employment practice for any person to aid, abet, incite, compel, or coerce the doing of any act forbidden by the Act, or to attempt to do so. The plaintiffs in Janken, and the plaintiff in Reno, argued that a supervisor who participates in a discriminatory personnel decision aids and abets the employer and is personally liable on that basis.

Reno reproduced and adopted Janken’s answer. The provision was read as reaching third parties such as customers or suppliers who induce or coerce prohibited discrimination; it was not read as making a corporate employee an aider and abettor of the corporation when the employee exercises delegated personnel management authority on the corporation’s behalf. The Court described the linguistic difficulty of saying that an employee exercising delegated authority “aids and abets” the employer in managing personnel, and concluded that had the Legislature meant to expose every person who makes personnel decisions in California to personal liability, it would have said so more directly.

RENO APPLIED THE SAME RULE TO THE COMMON LAW CLAIM FOR DISCHARGE IN VIOLATION OF PUBLIC POLICY
Reno’s plaintiff pleaded a second cause of action: discharge in violation of public policy, the tort recognized in Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (1980) 27 Cal.3d 167, with the FEHA supplying the public policy. The Court held that its FEHA conclusion carried over. Relying on Jennings v. Marralle (1994) 8 Cal.4th 121, where a defendant too small to be an “employer” under the FEHA could not be sued in tort on a public policy resting on the FEHA, the Court reasoned that it would be absurd to forbid suit against a supervisor under the statute and then permit essentially the same action under a different label.

The Court was explicit that it was not deciding the separate question whether discrimination based on medical condition is among the fundamental public policies that will support a Tameny action at all.

MIKLOSY V. REGENTS: THE TAMENY TORT LIES ONLY AGAINST AN EMPLOYER, WHATEVER PUBLIC POLICY IS INVOKED
Miklosy v. Regents of the University of California (2008) 44 Cal.4th 876 arose from whistleblower allegations by laboratory employees who sued the University and individual supervisors. After holding that Government Code section 815 barred a Tameny action against the public entity, the Court addressed the claims against the individuals and held that they failed for a reason independent of public-entity law.

The Court reasoned that the Tameny tort is premised on the wrongful termination of an employment relationship: the duty it enforces is a duty the law imposes on employers, and the breach of the employment relationship is an indispensable element because it is the instrument of the injury. An individual who is not an employer, the Court said, cannot commit the tort; he or she can only be the agent through which an employer commits it. The Court noted that the contrary Court of Appeal decision on which the plaintiffs relied had rested on the specific “person” language of the FEHA’s retaliation provision, and that it had rejected that reading earlier the same year in Jones v. Lodge at Torrey Pines Partnership.

JONES V. LODGE AT TORREY PINES PARTNERSHIP: THE SAME RULE GOVERNS FEHA RETALIATION, EVEN THOUGH THE STATUTE SAYS “PERSON”
The FEHA’s retaliation provision is worded differently from its discrimination provision. Government Code section 12940, subdivision (h), forbids retaliation by “any employer, labor organization, employment agency, or person,” while subdivision (a) reaches only “an employer.” In Jones v. Lodge at Torrey Pines Partnership (2008) 42 Cal.4th 1158, an employee who won a jury verdict against both his employer and his supervisor argued that the word “person” made the supervisor personally liable.

The Court held otherwise. It found the word ambiguous in context, observing that subdivision (h) is a catchall that protects a person who opposes any practice forbidden by the Act, and that each entity it names is the subject of some other subdivision, so that the list may simply conform to those other provisions. It then applied Reno’s reasoning, examined the legislative history of the 1987 bill that added “person” to the provision — which contemporaneous agency analyses described as technical clean-up legislation — and concluded that the employer, but not nonemployer individuals, is liable for retaliation. The Court disapproved two Court of Appeal decisions to the contrary.

WHAT THESE DECISIONS DID NOT DECIDE, AND THE CONTRAST WITH HARASSMENT
Both decisions marked the edges of what they held. Reno stated in a footnote that the case before it involved a claim for discrimination and not harassment, and that the Court expressed no opinion regarding individuals’ liability for harassment. In the body of the opinion the Court also declined to address the scope of employer liability under the FEHA for either discrimination or harassment, and specifically declined to say whether the “agent” language of the definition merely incorporates respondeat superior principles or means something else.

Ten years later, Jones described the harassment side of the line as settled in the opposite direction, noting that the Court had recognized that at least some individuals may be liable for harassment. The statutory basis for that difference is Government Code section 12940, subdivision (j)(3), which states in terms that an employee of a covered entity is personally liable for harassment the employee perpetrates, regardless of the employer’s knowledge or response — a provision with no counterpart in the discrimination or retaliation subdivisions.

Reno rested on a distinction the FEHA itself draws between harassment and discrimination. Quoting Janken, the Court explained that harassment consists of conduct outside the scope of necessary job performance, while making decisions is conduct essential to personnel management — a supervisor can refrain from harassing, but cannot refrain from making the personnel decisions that may later be claimed to be discriminatory. The same passage lists the kinds of actions the Legislature treated as commonly necessary personnel management: hiring and firing, job or project assignments, promotion or demotion, performance evaluations, and deciding who will be laid off.

The Court also gave a structural reason. Labor Code section 1102.5, the general whistleblower-retaliation statute, is worded differently again. Its operative subdivisions do not address an “employer” alone: subdivision (b) provides that an employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee for disclosing information the employee has reasonable cause to believe discloses a violation of law. The same formula appears in subdivisions (a), (c), (d) and (h), and subdivision (i) states that for purposes of the section “employer” or “a person acting on behalf of the employer” includes, but is not limited to, a client employer as defined in Labor Code section 2810.3.

The reasoning of Jones v. Lodge at Torrey Pines Partnership is a point of comparison rather than an answer. There the Court held that the FEHA’s use of the single word “person” in a list did not make nonemployer individuals liable, relying heavily on the absence of any legislative history suggesting the word was meant to create individual liability. Section 1102.5 uses a different and fuller phrase, and its present form comes from a later enactment; the clause below records what the statute says, and the gap records what the retrieved authorities do and do not decide about it.

citations.cite: Lab. Code § 1102.5, subd. (b)
citations.quote: An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee for disclosing information, or because the employer believes that the employee disclosed or may disclose information, to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee or another employee who has the authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance, or for providing information to, or testifying before, any public body conducting an investigation, hearing, or inquiry, if the employee has reasonable cause to believe that the information discloses a violation of state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation, regardless of whether disclosing the information is part of the employee’s job duties.
